passage:
For most of the last century the deaf households of Vallen, a fishing town of nine thousand on the north coast, used a sign language of their own. It was not taught anywhere. It passed between neighbours, at the quay and in kitchens, among perhaps three hundred people. In 1962 a schoolteacher named Hesper Lund began writing it down, and in 1968 she published the first dictionary of it.

The book was arranged in the way that seemed obvious. Each sign was listed under the nearest word of the national language, and the words ran from A to Z. To find the sign for “net” you looked under N. The reviews were admiring. Copies were bought by the schools, by the cottage hospital, and by the ferry office, where a clerk kept one under the counter.

The clerk could not use it. A dictionary is opened by somebody who has met a thing and does not know what it is, and what the clerk had met was a shape made by a hand. She could not look up “net,” because “net” was precisely what she did not have. The book could be used only by a person who already knew the answer to the question the book was for. Lund understood this within a year and said so in print, in terms her publisher thought needlessly severe.

The second edition, in 1974, was ordered by the hands. Lund sorted the signs first by the shape the hand was held in — flat, closed, one finger extended, and so on — then by the place on the body where the sign was made, then by the way it moved. Finding an entry now meant working from what you had seen toward what it meant. The scheme was harder to typeset and harder to learn than the alphabet, and Lund defended it on one ground only: that it ran in the direction a dictionary is actually used.

Reordering the book also corrected it. Under the alphabetical scheme one sign had been entered twice, eleven pages apart, once under “weather” and once under “wait,” because the national language has two words there and Lund had been following the words. Stood side by side by handshape, the two entries were one sign, which Vallen had always used for the long hold before a boat can safely go out. Three more pairs came apart the same way. The mistakes had not been mistakes of observation. They had been the index working backward into the entries.
prompt: The passage is chiefly concerned with
choices: how a language grew up in one town, and what outsiders had missed in it
how Lund’s first dictionary was received, and who chose to buy a copy
why a dictionary’s order decides who can use it, and what a new order uncovered
how signs are described on a page, and how many of them Lund collected
correct_answer: why a dictionary’s order decides who can use it, and what a new order uncovered
explanation: Four of the five paragraphs turn on the arrangement of the entries: the alphabetical scheme of the first edition, the clerk who could not enter the book by the only door it had, the handshape scheme of 1974, and the duplicated sign that the new order pulled into view. “Why a dictionary’s order decides who can use it, and what a new order uncovered” names both halves of that. The town’s language is set up in the first paragraph and then left; “how Lund’s first dictionary was received” covers four sentences of the second paragraph; and the passage never says how many signs Lund collected, so “how signs are described on a page, and how many of them Lund collected” asks for a figure the passage does not give.

prompt: In saying that the mistakes “had not been mistakes of observation,” the writer means that Lund had
choices: misread two signs that are made in similar ways

correct_answer: seen the signs correctly but filed them under the wrong headings

passage:
At the thirty-kilometre mark on the Bregg seafront, where the road turns and the crowd is thin, Anneli Kaas stands just off the white line with a yellow paddle in each hand. She has judged race walking for twenty-two years. Her whole task, for the four hours the race lasts, is to decide by eye whether the athletes going past her are still walking.

The rule she is applying has two halves. A walker must keep contact with the ground — some part of one foot touching — at every instant of the stride; and the forward leg must be straight from the moment it lands until it passes beneath the body. A judge who sees either half broken shows a paddle. Three paddles, from three different judges, and the walker is out of the race.

In 1991 a group at the Halbrecht institute filmed the finalists of a national championship at two thousand frames a second and counted. Every one of the twelve was off the ground for part of every stride, for between twenty and fifty thousandths of a second. Some of them were walkers no judge had ever flagged. By the letter of the rule, the whole final should have been disqualified, and so, presumably, should every race walked since the rule was written.

What the federation did next was called an evasion at the time. It rewrote the rule to require that contact be kept with no loss of it visible to the human eye. Critics said the sport had written cheating into its own book. Kaas has always answered that the rule had never meant anything else: what the camera exposed was not a generation of cheats but a sentence that had been describing a thing it had no way of measuring.

The amendment changed what a walker works at. It is not possible to train away fifty thousandths of a second; it is possible to train the stride until the break does not show, and that is what the good ones do. It changed the judges too, though no rule book says so. Kaas took her place at the turn, low and a little behind the walkers, because that is where a heel leaving the road shows against the surface. A judge standing square on at the finish straight, with the sun off the sea behind the athletes, sees a great deal less, and there is nothing in the book to stop her standing there.
prompt: According to the second paragraph, a walker is put out of the race when
choices: a single judge sees the forward leg bend as it lands
three different judges have each shown a paddle
one judge has shown a paddle at the same walker three times
the chief judge decides that contact has been lost
correct_answer: three different judges have each shown a paddle
explanation: The paragraph sets the threshold exactly: “Three paddles, from three different judges, and the walker is out of the race.” “A single judge sees the forward leg bend as it lands” is one paddle, not three; “one judge has shown a paddle at the same walker three times” keeps the count and drops the requirement that the judges be different, which is the part the sentence insists on; and no chief judge appears anywhere in the passage.

prompt: The third paragraph implies that before 1991 the judges had been
choices: overlooking breaks in contact that were plain to see
applying the contact rule more strictly to the leading walkers

correct_answer: flagging only some of the walkers who were in fact leaving the ground

passage:
At the thirty-kilometre mark on the Bregg seafront, where the road turns and the crowd is thin, Anneli Kaas stands just off the white line with a yellow paddle in each hand. She has judged race walking for twenty-two years. Her whole task, for the four hours the race lasts, is to decide by eye whether the athletes going past her are still walking.

The rule she is applying has two halves. A walker must keep contact with the ground — some part of one foot touching — at every instant of the stride; and the forward leg must be straight from the moment it lands until it passes beneath the body. A judge who sees either half broken shows a paddle. Three paddles, from three different judges, and the walker is out of the race.

In 1991 a group at the Halbrecht institute filmed the finalists of a national championship at two thousand frames a second and counted. Every one of the twelve was off the ground for part of every stride, for between twenty and fifty thousandths of a second. Some of them were walkers no judge had ever flagged. By the letter of the rule, the whole final should have been disqualified, and so, presumably, should every race walked since the rule was written.

What the federation did next was called an evasion at the time. It rewrote the rule to require that contact be kept with no loss of it visible to the human eye. Critics said the sport had written cheating into its own book. Kaas has always answered that the rule had never meant anything else: what the camera exposed was not a generation of cheats but a sentence that had been describing a thing it had no way of measuring.

The amendment changed what a walker works at. It is not possible to train away fifty thousandths of a second; it is possible to train the stride until the break does not show, and that is what the good ones do. It changed the judges too, though no rule book says so. Kaas took her place at the turn, low and a little behind the walkers, because that is where a heel leaving the road shows against the surface. A judge standing square on at the finish straight, with the sun off the sea behind the athletes, sees a great deal less, and there is nothing in the book to stop her standing there.
